title: DSOD: Learning Deeply Supervised Object Detectors from Scratch
venue: IEEE International Conference on Computer Vision (ICCV)

problem.summary: State-of-the-art detectors all fine-tune networks pre-trained on ImageNet classification, which the authors argue limits structure design space, biases optimization toward a classification-tuned solution, and breaks down when source and target domains differ (RGB vs. depth, medical, multi-spectral images).
statements: Object detectors depend on off-the-shelf ImageNet pre-trained networks, restricting how detector architectures can be designed and how much compute they use.

Because loss functions and category distributions differ between classification and detection, fine-tuning starts learning in a biased optimization space that may be a poor local minimum for detection.
Domain mismatch makes transferring classification pre-training to depth, medical or multi-spectral detection inputs unreliable.
Previous attempts to train detectors from scratch failed because of more complicated loss functions and limited detection training data.

evidence.quote: A better solution to tackle these two critical problems is to train object detectors from scratch, which motivates our proposed DSOD.
However, there are also critical limitations when adopting the pre-trained networks in object detection: (1) Limited structure design space.

(2) Learning bias. As both the loss functions and the category distributions between classification and detection tasks are different, we argue that this will lead to different searching/optimization spaces.
Previous efforts in this direction mostly failed due to much more complicated loss functions and limited training data in object detection.

background.summary: The paper builds on the SSD single-shot framework for speed, DenseNet for deep layer-wise supervision, and the R-CNN/Fast R-CNN/Faster R-CNN/R-FCN and YOLO/SSD families as the detection landscape. The claimed gap is that no prior work trains an object detection network from scratch.

relatedWork.name: SSD
relatedWork.relation: the single-shot, proposal-free framework DSOD is built on for its speed/accuracy trade-off
relatedWork.quote: Our proposed DSOD is built upon the SSD framework and thus it inherits the speed and accuracy advantages of SSD, while produces smaller and more flexible models.

relatedWork.name: DenseNet
relatedWork.relation: source of the dense layer-wise connections that provide implicit deep supervision
relatedWork.quote: A block is called dense block when all preceding layers in the block are connected to the current layer.

relatedWork.name: Faster R-CNN / R-FCN
relatedWork.relation: region-proposal-based detectors with integrated RPNs; failed to converge when trained from scratch
relatedWork.quote: Proposal based methods include R-CNN [5], Fast RCNN [4], Faster R-CNN [27] and R-FCN [19].

relatedWork.name: YOLO / SSD
relatedWork.relation: single-shot proposal-free detectors, the category the authors found trainable from scratch
relatedWork.quote: YOLO and SSD are single-shot and proposal-free methods, which handle object location and bounding box coordinates as a regression problem.

evidence.quote: Most detection methods [5, 4, 27, 21] directly utilize pre-trained ImageNet models as the backbone network.
To the best of our knowledge, there are no works which train object detection networks from scratch.

solution.summary: DSOD is a proposal-free, SSD-style multi-scale detector trained entirely from scratch, using a deeply supervised DenseNet-style backbone plus a dense front-end prediction structure. Dense layer-wise connections deliver deep supervision so earlier layers still receive gradient signal from the single top loss.
solution.approach: Combine a proposal-free SSD-style detector with dense layer-wise connections in both the backbone and the multi-scale prediction layers, giving implicit deep supervision that lets the network converge from random initialization.
components: proposal-free multi-scale detection framework derived from SSD
deeply supervised DenseNet-style backbone (stem block, four dense blocks, transition layers)
transition w/o pooling layers to add dense blocks without shrinking feature-map resolution
stem block of three 3x3 convolutions plus 2x2 max pooling to reduce early information loss
dense front-end prediction layers that learn half the feature maps and reuse half from preceding scales
L2 normalization of feature norms to 20 on all prediction outputs

evidence.quote: One of the key findings is that deep supervision, enabled by dense layer-wise connections, plays a critical role in learning a good detector.
Hence, we arrive at the first principle: training detection network from scratch requires a proposal-free framework.
For each scale, we only learn half of new feature maps and reuse the remaining half of the previous ones.
This dense prediction structure can yield more accurate results with fewer parameters than the plain structure

experiments.summary: The paper reports controlled ablations on PASCAL VOC 2007 for each design principle, then full evaluations on PASCAL VOC 2007/2012 and MS COCO with mAP, comparing against SSD, Faster R-CNN, R-FCN and YOLOv2 in both accuracy, parameters and FPS.

benchmarks.split: 300x300 input, dense prediction layers, Titan X

evidence.quote: Experiments on PASCAL VOC 2007, 2012 and MS COCO datasets demonstrate that DSOD can achieve better results than the state-of-the-art solutions with much more compact models.
Our DSOD300 achieves 77.7% mAP, which is much better than the SSD300S that is trained from scratch using VGG16 (69.6%)
After adding COCO as training data, the performance is further improved to 81.7%.

limitations.summary: From-scratch training is restricted to proposal-free frameworks (RoI pooling blocked gradient flow in two-stage variants tested), the 300x300 input hurts small-object precision relative to larger-input detectors, and the dense prediction head costs some speed.
items: Small-object detection precision on COCO lags R-FCN because DSOD uses 300x300 inputs versus roughly 600x1000 for R-FCN.
The dense front-end prediction structure runs slower than the plain SSD structure (17.4 fps vs. 20.6 fps) due to extra down-sampling blocks.
Faster R-CNN and R-FCN variants attempted from scratch failed to converge with every backbone tried (VGGNet, ResNet, DenseNet).
The behavior of ImageNet pre-training for DSOD-style backbones was only probed with one small backbone and left unexplained.

evidence.quote: It is reasonable that our small object detection precision is slightly lower than R-FCN since our input image size (300×300) is much smaller than R-FCN's (∼ 600×1000).
DSOD with dense front-end structure runs slightly lower than the plain structure (17.4 fps vs. 20.6 fps) on a Titan X GPU, due to the overhead from additional down-sampling blocks.
However, the training process failed to converge for all the network structures we attempted (VGGNet, ResNet, DenseNet).

futureDirections.direction: Apply from-scratch training to non-RGB domains (depth, medical, multi-spectral imagery) where ImageNet pre-training does not transfer.
futureDirections.quote: Our future work will consider these domains, as well as learning ultra efficient DSOD models to support resource-bounded devices.

futureDirections.direction: Clarify whether pre-training the DSOD backbone on ImageNet helps or not, which the single probe left open.
futureDirections.quote: Future work will investigate this point more thoroughly.

applications.detail: The paper frames object detection as a fast-moving area with wide industrial applications in surveillance and autonomous driving.
applications.quote: Among them, object detection is one of the fastest moving areas due to its wide applications in surveillance, autonomous driving, etc.

applications.detail: Freedom from heavy pre-trained backbones is presented as critical for deploying detectors on resource-constrained IoT hardware.
applications.quote: This is very critical for the deployment of deep neural networks models to resource-limited Internet-of-Things (IoT) scenario.

applications.detail: A 5.9M-parameter variant reaching 73.6% mAP is highlighted as suitable for low-end devices such as mobile phones and embedded electronics.
applications.quote: our smallest dense model (DS/64-64-16-1, with dense prediction layers) achieves 73.6% mAP with only 5.9M parameters, which shows great potential for applications on low-end devices

deploymentClaims: DSOD runs at 20.6 fps (48.6 ms/image) with plain prediction layers and 17.4 fps (57.5 ms/image) with dense prediction layers on a single Titan X GPU.
A lite version with 10.4M parameters runs at 25.8 fps with only a 1% mAP drop.
57.5 ms per image on one Titan X GPU or 590 ms on an Intel Core i7-5960X CPU at 3.00GHz.
Model size is about 1/2 of SSD300, 1/4 of R-FCN and 1/10 of Faster R-CNN.

evidence.quote: For instance, DSOD outperforms SSD on all three benchmarks with real-time detection speed, while requires only 1/2 parameters to SSD and 1/10 parameters to Faster RCNN.
our full DSOD can process an image in 48.6ms (20.6 fps) on a single Titan X GPU with the plain prediction structure
